lessons.title: Indices, surds and exponential equations

lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Rationalise denominators with surds and find unknown rational numbers.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Equal bases
blocks.md: If $a^x = a^y$ (a > 0, a ≠ 1) then x = y. So write both sides with the **same base**: $4^x = 8$ becomes $2^{2x} = 2^3$ and x = 3/2. When the bases cannot match, take logarithms.

blocks.title: Rationalising and equating
blocks.md: Multiply top and bottom by the **conjugate**: for $\frac{1}{a - \sqrt{b}}$ multiply by $a + \sqrt{b}$, using $(a - \sqrt{b})(a + \sqrt{b}) = a^2 - b$. If $p + q\sqrt{3} = r + s\sqrt{3}$ with rational p, q, r, s then p = r and q = s.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Adding the indices when bases are different.
- Multiplying by the same surd instead of the conjugate: $\frac{1}{3 - \sqrt{5}} \times \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}}$ does not remove the root.
- Forgetting that $3^x > 0$: negative solutions for $3^x$ are rejected.

blocks.title: Example 1: exponential equations
steps: (b) Put u = 3ˣ, so 9ˣ = u². Then u² − 4u + 3 = 0, (u − 1)(u − 3) = 0, so u = 1 or 3.

blocks.title: Example 2: surds
blocks.statement: Express $\frac{1}{3 - \sqrt{5}}$ with a rational denominator, and find rational a and b with $\frac{2 + \sqrt{3}}{2 - \sqrt{3}} = a + b\sqrt{3}$.

lessons.title: Logarithms
lessons.programRef: O Level Further Mathematics — Indices, surds, logarithms (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State and use the laws of logarithms.
Solve equations involving logarithms and exponentials.
Change the base of a logarithm.
reviewNotes: Natural logarithms (ln, base e) may also appear; the lesson uses base 10 and general bases only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.md: $\log_a b = c$ means $a^c = b$ (a > 0, a ≠ 1, b > 0). Examples: $\log_2 8 = 3$ because $2^3 = 8$; $\log 1000 = 3$ (log with no base means base 10); $\log_a 1 = 0$ and $\log_a a = 1$.

blocks.title: Laws of logarithms
blocks.md:
- $\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y$
- $\log_a\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = \log_a x - \log_a y$
- $\log_a(x^n) = n\log_a x$
- Change of base: $\log_a b = \frac{\log b}{\log a}$

blocks.title: Method: solving
blocks.md: To solve $a^x = b$, take logs of both sides: $x = \frac{\log b}{\log a}$. For an equation with logs, combine them into **one** log, convert to an index equation, solve, then **reject** values that make a log argument zero or negative.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- $\log(x + y) \neq \log x + \log y$.
- $\frac{\log x}{\log y} \neq \log x - \log y$.
- Forgetting to check the solutions: the argument of a log must be positive.

blocks.title: Example 1: an exponential equation
blocks.statement: Solve $2^x = 7$ to 3 significant figures, and find $\log_2 8 + \log_2 4$.

blocks.title: Example 2: a logarithm equation
steps: x = −2 makes $\log_2 x$ undefined: reject. Check x = 4: log₂4 + log₂2 = 2 + 1 = 3.
